name: Modern Defence (rare)
summary: Black skips the usual central pawn moves, fianchettoes the bishop and lets White build a big center, then attacks it. A rare setup that many players at this level have never faced.

goal.title: Fianchetto the bishop, let White build, then strike the center
goal.text: Black skips the usual central pawn moves. The king-side bishop goes to the long diagonal behind a pawn, the pieces come out in a flexible way, and Black castles early. White often builds a large pawn center in reply, and Black's plan is to attack that center from the side with pawn breaks and the long-range bishop.
plans: Push the g-pawn one step to open the long diagonal and put the king-side bishop there.
Develop the king-side knight and a modest center pawn, then castle early.
Let White build the center, then hit it with a side pawn or a central pawn break at the right moment.
Keep the long-diagonal bishop as your best piece. Only put a pawn in its way when that pawn is fighting for the center, and expect the diagonal to reopen later.
goal.narration: Welcome to the Modern Defence. The idea is simple, and a little sneaky. Black does not rush a pawn into the center. Instead, the king's bishop slides onto the long diagonal behind a pawn, the knight and a modest center pawn follow, and Black castles early. White is invited to build a big pawn center, and that is the point, because a big center can become a target. Black attacks it from the side, with a pawn break at the right moment and with the bishop on the long diagonal, which gets stronger every time a central pawn disappears. As you watch, keep asking one question: what is that bishop looking at, and what is standing in its way?

variations.name: 1.e4 g6 2.d4: the classical setup
variations.strategy: White has built a big center and both sides have castled, so the middlegame is about attacking that center. Strike with a pawn break, the c-pawn or the e-pawn push depending on where White's pieces stand, and let the long-diagonal bishop come alive once pawns are traded. Do not be passive: White's space can turn into a king-side attack if you wait too long, so choose your break, prepare it and play it.

moves.narration: White opens by grabbing space in the center with the king's pawn. It is the most popular first move in chess, and Black's setup is built to meet it.

moves.note: Prepare the bishop for the long diagonal. Few players at this level know how to meet it.
moves.narration: Here is the signature move. The g-pawn steps up one square, which opens the diagonal for the king's bishop. It looks odd, but few players at this level have faced it, so you will know more than your opponent.
White builds the big center, with pawns on d4 and e4. Do not worry, this is exactly what the setup invites. Those pawns need defending, and they are what Black will aim at later.

moves.note: The bishop takes the long diagonal.

mistakes.text: Not a blunder, but wasted time: the knight attacks d4, yet d5 kicks it away and White gains space and a tempo.

moves.narration: The bishop lands on the long diagonal, pointing at the center and the far corner of the board. Most of Black's play comes from this one piece. A common slip here is knight to c6, hitting the d4 pawn. It is not a blunder, but White just plays d5, the knight has to move again, and White gains space and a tempo.
White develops the queen's knight. It supports the e-pawn and brings another piece into the game.

moves.note: Make room for the knight and keep your options open.

mistakes.text: Hitting the e-pawn too early lets White gain a tempo with e5: your knight is driven back and White has more space.

moves.narration: A quiet move with a purpose. The d-pawn steps up one square, which keeps the position flexible and covers the e5 square. A common slip is to play the knight to f6 right away. Then White pushes the e-pawn, the knight is driven back, and White has more space.
White develops the second knight. It covers the center and gets ready for castling.

mistakes.text: Opening the center early lets the queens come off with check. Your king loses the right to castle and White's pieces get ahead.

moves.narration: Now the knight comes out and attacks the e-pawn, so White has to respond. A tempting but poor idea here is to open the center at once with e5. After the trades, the queens come off with check, Black's king can no longer castle, and White's pieces are ahead.

moves.note: White defends the e-pawn by developing.
moves.narration: White defends the e-pawn by developing the bishop. It is also a step toward castling.

mistakes.text: Opening the center early lets the queens come off with check. Your king loses the right to castle and the e5 pawn falls.

moves.narration: Black castles, and the king is safe behind the bishop on the long diagonal. Again, resist the urge to play e5 right now. With the pieces not ready, White simply wins that pawn.
White castles as well. Both kings are safe, development is nearly done, and the real middlegame battle is about to begin.

moves.note: Stay flexible: this prepares a central break or queen-side expansion.
moves.narration: And here is the flexible move, c6. It prepares a central break with the d-pawn or the e-pawn, and it gives Black room to expand on the queen-side. From here the plan is yours: choose a break, prepare it, and strike before White's space becomes an attack. When the center opens, that bishop on the long diagonal comes alive.

variations.narration: Now the line itself. White plays the classical setup, with pawns on e4 and d4, both knights out, a bishop developed, and a castled king. Black answers in the same calm way. After that, the middlegame is a fight about White's center. Do not be passive, because White's space can turn into a king-side attack if you wait too long. Choose a pawn break, either the d-pawn or the e-pawn, prepare it, and play it. Once pawns come off, the long-diagonal bishop wakes up.

variations.name: 1.e4 g6 2.d4 with f4: the Austrian Attack
variations.strategy: White's f-pawn makes the center look huge, but it loosens White's king side. Black hits the center at once and trades off White's d-pawn, so the big center shrinks to two pawns. Castle quickly: White's main idea is to push the e-pawn to kick your king-side knight, and until that knight moves your long-diagonal bishop is blocked. Develop the queen-side knight, aim at White's e-pawn, and use the loosened king side as a target once the bishop comes alive.

moves.note: Material is level and White's center is down to two pawns.

variations.name: 1.e4 g6 2.d4 with c4: a big center
variations.strategy: This is a King's Indian-style structure where White has a lot of space. Black has castled and keeps the king safe while pressuring White's d-pawn with the queen-side knight; the long-diagonal bishop joins in once the king-side knight moves or the center opens. Break with the e-pawn when your pieces are ready, or with a queen-side pawn push. If White castles on the queen side, a pawn storm against it is Black's plan. Don't trade your long-diagonal bishop without a good reason.

moves.note: White adds the c-pawn for even more space.

variations.name: 1.e4 g6 2.Bc4: the quiet bishop
variations.strategy: White has no big center, so the middlegame is quieter and you can take space yourself. Your king is safe, and the long-diagonal bishop becomes strong once the center opens, so aim for the central pawn push supported by the knights. Watch White's bishop on the king-side diagonal, but it has little to hit once your king is castled. If you gain space, avoid unnecessary trades; if you get cramped, trade pieces. Keep the position flexible.

White develops the bishop toward your king side.
The bishop still takes the long diagonal.

mistakes.text: The e4 pawn is guarded by the d-pawn and the knight, so this just gives a knight for a pawn.
Pushing d5 loses a pawn: after the trades the pawn on d5 is attacked more often than it is defended.

variations.name: 1.e4 g6 2.Nc3: the f-pawn plan
variations.strategy: White pushes the f-pawn to grab space in the center and aims the bishop at your king side. Castle early: the f-pawn is then defended by the king and rook. Once White has castled too, look for the central knight capture: if White's pieces are loose, a pawn push forks the bishop and the knight and you win the material back. The long-diagonal bishop and a later central break are your trumps.

variations.name: 1.d4 g6 2.c4: the King's Indian setup
variations.strategy: White has the space and Black has the long diagonal and the e-pawn break. After the central break the tension is in the center: decide whether to trade pawns or keep it closed. If the center locks, White plays on the queen side and Black attacks White's king with the f-pawn push. Keep the long-diagonal bishop flexible, and use the knights on the central outposts.

variations.name: 1.d4 g6 2.Nf3 with the London bishop
variations.strategy: White has no big center, so both sides develop calmly. You have castled and the long-diagonal bishop is ready. Challenge White's bishop and center with the e-pawn push, or hit the center with the c-pawn push. If White's bishop retreats, take the extra space. Keep the pieces coordinated and don't rush: you are not worse.

variations.name: 1.Nf3 g6 2.g3: a flexible mirror
variations.strategy: Black has claimed the center with the e-pawn while White keeps a flexible setup. Support the center pawns with the knights and the c-pawn, use the long-diagonal bishop, and look for the f-pawn push to expand. White's bishop on the long diagonal also looks at your queen side, so keep your pieces coordinated there.

variations.name: 1.c4 g6 2.Nc3: mirror the setup
variations.strategy: Both sides are fianchettoed, so the middlegame is about the central break. Develop the knights, castle, and prepare the d-pawn push to claim space in the center. Hit the queen-side with pieces and pawns if White commits there. The long-diagonal bishop is your best piece, so keep it open and trade into a position you understand.
